entities.name: Abdi-Milkutti
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abdi-Milkutti was a King of Sidon who rose up against Assyrian rule during the Classical era, becoming a significant figure in the power dynamics between regional kingdoms and the expanding Neo-Assyrian Empire. He had formed a strategic military alliance with Sanduarri, king of Kundi and Sizu, a prince of the Lebanon, probably during the time of the civil war waged between Esarhaddon and two of his brothers who disputed his succession after they had murdered his father. The two kings had sworn to each other by the names of the great gods and revolted, demonstrating the complex political systems and geopolitical linkages that characterized this period of imperial expansion.

As soon as this internal Assyrian struggle was over, in response to the rebellion, Esarhaddon launched a massive military campaign and laid siege to Sidon, which after three years of siege, in 677 BC, was finally captured, destroyed and rebuilt as Kar-Ashur-aha-iddina, the Harbour of Esarhaddon. This event represents a critical moment in the establishment of Assyrian dynastic legacies and territorial boundaries. The Sidonian king Abdi-Milkutti was decapitated. Sanduarri was also captured and decapitated, and the heads of the two kings were hung around the necks of their nobles who were paraded through the streets of Nineveh as a display of imperial power and deterrence. Part of the treasure taken from Sidon went to the loyal king of the rival city Tyre, reinforcing the hierarchical system of imperial authority and reward. Abdi-Milkutti's rebellion and its consequences contributed significantly to the enduring intellectual and institutional frameworks that shaped subsequent civilizations, particularly in demonstrating the overwhelming military superiority of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and the futility of regional resistance against imperial consolidation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abdi-Milkutti's rebellion against Assyrian rule led to a three-year siege of Sidon, resulting in its destruction and rebuilding as Kar-Ashur-aha-iddina. The event highlights the power dynamics between regional kingdoms during the Neo-Assyrian Empire.
